# Topic at a Glance

> **One-sentence summary:** A k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graph connects every observation to a small set of its most similar observations, preserving local structure without claiming that all samples belong to a global geometry or a fixed set of clusters.

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| **Biological question** | Which cells, samples, or molecular profiles have similar local states? |
| **Computational problem** | Build a sparse neighborhood graph from high-dimensional observations or an embedding |
| **Method type** | Graph construction and nonparametric neighborhood modeling |
| **Input** | Feature matrix or usually a preprocessed low-dimensional representation, a metric, and $k$ |
| **Output** | A sparse adjacency/weight matrix, connected components, and neighborhoods for downstream algorithms |
| **Uses** | Single-cell neighbors, label transfer, graph clustering, manifold learning, and trajectory inference |
| **Prerequisites** | Distance metrics, normalization, and [principal component analysis](principal-component-analysis-for-omics-data.qmd) |

# From profiles to local neighborhoods

An expression profile, genotype vector, or protein embedding has many coordinates, but many analyses only need to know which observations are nearby. A kNN graph keeps that information compactly. For each observation $i$, compute its distances to the other observations and add edges from $i$ to the $k$ closest ones.

```text
normalized feature matrix
    -> choose representation and distance metric
    -> find k nearest neighbors of each observation
    -> symmetrize and optionally weight edges
    -> sparse neighborhood graph
    -> clustering, visualization, smoothing, or trajectories
```

The word *nearest* is meaningful only relative to the chosen representation and metric. In single-cell RNA-seq, Euclidean neighbors in a PCA representation of selected variable genes are common; nearest neighbors of raw counts or an uncorrected batch-dominated embedding can instead reflect sequencing depth or technical batch.

# The graph definition and its choices

Let $z_i$ denote the representation of observation $i$ and $d(z_i,z_j)$ a distance. Its directed neighbor set is

$$
N_k(i)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{i\},\,|S|=k}\sum_{j\in S}d(z_i,z_j).
$$

Set $A_{ij}=1$ when $j\in N_k(i)$ to obtain a directed graph. Downstream software often makes it undirected using either rule below.

| Rule | Edge retained when | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Union / symmetric kNN | $i$ chooses $j$ **or** $j$ chooses $i$ | Retains more links and can connect varying-density regions |
| Mutual kNN | $i$ chooses $j$ **and** $j$ chooses $i$ | Removes one-sided links but can fragment sparse populations |
| Weighted kNN | An edge is assigned a similarity from distance or shared neighbors | Lets close neighbors contribute more than marginal ones |

Many modern single-cell workflows use a shared-nearest-neighbor or fuzzy-simplicial weight rather than a binary edge. This reduces the influence of a pair that is close in isolation but does not share a neighborhood. It does not eliminate the need to inspect preprocessing and batch structure.

# A toy example

Suppose six cells have already been projected onto one informative coordinate:

| Cell | Coordinate |
|---|---:|
| A | 0.0 |
| B | 0.2 |
| C | 0.4 |
| D | 2.0 |
| E | 2.1 |
| F | 2.3 |

With $k=2$, A connects to B and C; B connects to A and C; D connects to E and F; and so on. The graph has two dense local components, suggesting two separated neighborhoods. If an additional cell at 1.1 is included, it can link the groups depending on $k$ and the symmetrization rule. That bridge may represent a biological transition, a doublet, or simply an undersampled gap; the graph alone cannot decide.

# Choosing the representation, metric, and $k$

The graph is a modeling layer, not a neutral preprocessing convenience.

| Choice | Consequence | Practical check |
|---|---|---|
| Features / embedding | Defines which differences count as nearby | Compare neighbors with known QC and biological metadata |
| Metric | Euclidean, cosine, correlation, and other metrics favor different shapes | State the metric and match it to the representation |
| $k$ | Small $k$ emphasizes fine local detail; large $k$ smooths across neighborhoods | Examine stability over a modest, predeclared range |
| Edge weighting | Changes graph connectivity and downstream optimization | Record whether edges are binary, distance-based, or shared-neighbor weights |
| Approximate search | Speeds large datasets but can miss some true neighbors | Measure recall or repeat with a controlled exact subset when feasible |

There is no universally correct $k$. Too small a value can leave many disconnected components and magnify sampling noise. Too large a value can create edges across distinct cell states, rare populations, or batches. Density also matters: a fixed $k$ reaches farther in sparse regions than in dense ones, so graph edges do not have a uniform biological scale.

# What kNN graphs enable

Once a graph is built, many methods operate on its adjacency $A$ or graph Laplacian $L=D-A$, where $D$ is the diagonal degree matrix.

| Downstream task | How the graph is used | Important caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Graph clustering | Find densely connected communities | A community is algorithm- and resolution-dependent, not automatically a cell type |
| UMAP or t-SNE preparation | Preserve selected local relationships in two dimensions | A display is not an independent validation of the graph |
| Diffusion / trajectory methods | Propagate local transitions across paths | Branches can reflect density, batch, or missing states |
| Label transfer | Assign labels by neighboring reference observations | Transfer uncertainty and detect out-of-reference cells |
| Smoothing / imputation | Average signal over neighbors | Can blur real boundaries and inflate apparent gene coexpression |

The graph complements global approaches. [PCA](principal-component-analysis-for-omics-data.qmd) describes axes of variation across all samples; [hierarchical clustering](hierarchical-clustering.qmd) builds a global nested tree; kNN graphs concentrate on local adjacency. The next note, [t-SNE dimensionality reduction](t-sne-dimensionality-reduction.qmd), uses neighbor probabilities to create a two-dimensional visualization.

# Diagnostics and failure modes

| Observation | Likely issue | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Neighbors are dominated by batch or library size | Representation retained technical variation | Revisit QC, normalization, integration strategy, and study design |
| Many tiny components | $k$ too small, sparse sampling, or a poor metric | Inspect component size and neighbor distances before increasing $k$ blindly |
| Rare group disappears after graph-based smoothing or clustering | Neighborhood spans the rare group into a larger population | Inspect the original graph and marker evidence at several settings |
| Nearly all nodes connect across known distinct controls | $k$ too large or embedding over-compressed | Reduce $k$, examine more PCs/features, and check distances |
| Different software gives different graphs | Different approximate search, metric, symmetrization, or weights | Record software version and all graph-construction parameters |

Neighbor graphs also suffer in high dimensions: distances can become less discriminative, and nuisance features can dominate. Dimensionality reduction can help, but reducing too aggressively can remove rare or continuous biology. A graph should therefore be audited with the representation and metadata from which it was made.

# Take-home Messages

1. A kNN graph is a sparse statement about local similarity, defined by representation, metric, $k$, and edge construction.
2. It is a central intermediate object for modern single-cell clustering, visualization, trajectory, and label-transfer workflows.
3. Small and large $k$ values trade local sensitivity against robustness and connectivity; report and assess the choice.
4. Graph structure can reflect technical variation or sampling density, so biological labels require independent evidence.
